summary:
IGNIS is an evidence-first web dashboard that makes NASA's microgravity combustion research usable for fire-safety decisions on future crewed missions. We turned 13 Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) investigations, including FLEX, BASS, SAFFIRE, ACME, SPICE and SLICE, into structured, provenance-tagged knowledge records. These are linked to flight hardware (CIR, MSG, MDCA) and to fire-safety concepts such as flame spread, detection and suppression.

Users choose a mission scenario: the ISS cabin, a lunar habitat, a pressurized rover, a spacesuit, or a Mars base. IGNIS then ranks which investigations tested comparable conditions, such as oxygen level, pressure and flow, and explains why each one matches. Just as important, it shows where no evidence exists. An Evidence Desk answers questions using only cited, verified sources and says "insufficient evidence" rather than guessing. Results can be exported as CSV or JSON for predictive modelling, and a live console summarizes each scenario.

This matters because fire behaves very differently in microgravity, and a fire in a sealed spacecraft or habitat can be catastrophic. Decades of NASA experiments are scattered across papers and datasets. IGNIS shows engineers and researchers what the evidence supports, what it doesn't, and where the next experiments or fire-control equipment should focus.
details:
IGNIS is a web dashboard that connects NASA's microgravity combustion research to fire-safety decisions for future crewed missions. We turned 13 NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) investigations, including FLEX, FLEX-2, BASS, BASS-II, SAFFIRE, ACME, CFI, SPICE, SLICE and SAME, into open, structured knowledge records. Each record captures the test conditions, such as oxygen, pressure, airflow, gravity, material, fuel and measurements, and notes where every value came from and whether it has been reviewed. The records link to the flight hardware used, such as the Combustion Integrated Rack, the Microgravity Science Glovebox and the Multi-user Droplet Combustion Apparatus, and to fire-safety concepts like flame spread, detection and suppression.

A user picks a mission setting, such as the ISS cabin, a lunar habitat, a pressurized rover, a spacesuit or a Mars base, or enters their own conditions. IGNIS then ranks which investigations tested similar conditions using a published, weighted scoring method. Each match is labeled as direct, related, bounding or unknown, and unknown values never earn credit. It also maps the gaps where NASA evidence is thin and suggests research questions, clearly marked as written by our team. An Evidence Desk answers plain-language questions by searching the records and writing a short answer that cites only those sources. If the sources don't support an answer, it says the evidence is insufficient rather than guessing. Users can also compare investigations side by side, analyze scenarios in a live console, and export the data as CSV or JSON for predictive modeling.

This matters because fire behaves very differently without gravity. Flames can burn cooler, spread more slowly, last longer and be harder to detect, and a fire in a sealed spacecraft or habitat leaves the crew nowhere to go. Decades of NASA experiments hold the answers, but they are spread across papers and datasets. IGNIS helps engineers, mission planners and researchers see quickly what the evidence supports for their conditions, what it does not, and how much to trust it. Our goal is to point new experiments, predictive models and fire-control equipment at the real gaps for Moon and Mars missions.

We built IGNIS in TypeScript with Next.js, React, Tailwind CSS, Recharts and GSAP, and stored the knowledge base as Markdown files checked with Zod. Search runs on Supabase with PostgreSQL and pgvector, using the BAAI bge-small-en-v1.5 model through Transformers.js to match questions by meaning. Answers come from an optional language model on Groq, and every answer is checked against its sources before it is shown. We tested the app with Vitest, ESLint, Prettier, automatic checks on every knowledge record, and a set of test questions. On those 27 questions, the right investigation came up first 93% of the time and was always in the top five. The app is hosted on Vercel and needs no special hardware, just a web browser.

What makes IGNIS creative is that it shows where the evidence runs out, not just what it says. Every value shows whether NASA measured it directly or our team interpreted it. The scores measure how similar the evidence is to a scenario, never fire risk, and the gap map turns missing evidence into a useful result. Mission presets put NASA's orbital and ground research in the setting of future habitats and rovers. The knowledge base is plain Markdown that anyone can read, check and extend.

Our team put scientific honesty first: no invented values and a clear line between NASA evidence and our own interpretation. We present IGNIS as a research aid, not a safety certification tool or an official NASA product. We published the scoring weights and made every source traceable. The app still works without the database or the language model, runs on free hosting with a small model, and needs no login. We split the work across five roles, with authors writing records and a separate member reviewing them. The site also works on phones and in both light and dark mode.
